steps.prompt: What does it actually take to build a game?
steps.sub: Not one giant app — three tools, each doing one job, handing off to the next. By the end you'll name all three, know what each is for, and trace how a model becomes a playable game.

steps.prompt: First instinct — which single tool builds a whole flat-screen game by itself?

options.t: Blender — it makes the 3D models, so it must run the game too.
None of them alone — you combine three tools, each doing one part.
Unity — it has everything, so you never need anything else.

steps.why: No single tool does it all well. You make assets in one (Blender), run the game in another (Unity), and write the behaviour code with a third (an AI coding agent). Blender can't run gameplay; Unity can host code but you still have to write it. The stack is the point.
hints: Each tool here is great at ONE thing and weak at the others.
Think 'assets', 'engine', and 'code' — that's three different jobs.

steps.sub: Tap each card. These three are your whole stack.

cards.b: Makes the 3D stuff: characters, props, environments. Then exports them out as files.
The engine. It assembles the scene, runs physics, draws every frame, and builds the final game.
Writes the C# scripts — the behaviour, like 'jump on spacebar' — from your plain-English description.

steps.prompt: Whose job is it? Sort each task to the right tool.
steps.sub: Tap a task, then tap the tool that owns it.

items.t: Run physics so the ship collides with asteroids
Write the C# that fires a laser on click

hints: If it's about SHAPING 3D geometry, it's Blender. If it's about RUNNING the game, it's Unity.
Anything that is a script / behaviour / rule written in C# is the coding agent's job.

steps.prompt: You modelled a hero in Blender. To get it into the game, what has to happen next?
steps.sub: Think about the hand-off between tools.

options.t: Nothing — Unity reads Blender's mind and the model just appears.
Export the model from Blender, then import that file into Unity.
Re-model the whole hero again from scratch inside Unity.

steps.why: Tools hand off through files. Blender exports the model (FBX or GLTF), and Unity imports that file into the project. You never rebuild the model in Unity — you bring it across. (That import step is its own lesson.)
hints: The tools don't share memory — they share files.
One side exports, the other side imports.

steps.prompt: Tap the hand-offs in the order a model travels to become playable.
steps.sub: Each tool finishes its job, then passes to the next.
chips: Unity runs the scene; the coding agent's script makes the hero move
Blender models the hero and exports it
Unity imports the model into the scene
hints: Start with where the asset is born.
Make it → bring it in → make it do something.

steps.sub: Tap True or False for each, then check all at once.

statements.t: Unity is where the model is shaped and sculpted, vertex by vertex.
statements.why: No — shaping geometry is Blender's job. Unity assembles and runs; it isn't a modelling tool.

statements.t: The AI coding agent writes the C# behaviour so you don't hand-type all of it.
statements.why: Right — you describe the behaviour in plain English and the agent writes the script. You still test and tweak it.

statements.t: You could skip Blender and still make a game with just boxes and spheres.
statements.why: True — Unity has built-in primitive shapes. Many first games are pure cubes. Blender matters once you want custom art.

statements.t: Each tool keeps the others' files in sync automatically over the internet.
statements.why: No — the hand-off is manual: you export from one tool and import into the next. Nothing syncs on its own.

hints: Map each claim back to the three cards: who shapes, who runs, who codes?
Remember the hand-off is files you move yourself.

steps.prompt: A beginner says: 'I'll just learn Unity and ignore the other two.' What breaks first?
steps.sub: Think about what Unity alone can and can't give you.

options.t: Nothing — Unity alone is genuinely enough for any game.
You'll have an engine but no custom art and no behaviour code — an empty stage.
Unity refuses to open without Blender installed.

steps.why: Unity is the stage and the projector — but a stage with no actors and no script is just an empty room. You still need assets (Blender, or primitives) and behaviour (the coding agent writes the C#). Learning all three is what makes a real game.
hints: Unity runs the game — but runs WHAT, exactly?
An engine with no art and no code has nothing to show or do.

steps.sub: Not graded. Picture the game you want to build — we'll keep tailoring examples to it.

fields.label: In one line, what game do you want to build?
fields.ph: e.g. a top-down maze where a cat dodges robots

fields.label: Name one custom asset you'd model in Blender for it:
fields.ph: e.g. the cat character / a glowing key / a spaceship

steps.prompt: Build the stack: tap the three tools that make a flat-screen game.
steps.sub: Some of these are real software but aren't part of this core stack. Pick only the three.
steps.why: The core stack is Blender + Unity + an AI coding agent: make the assets, run them in the engine, and write the behaviour. Photoshop or a video editor can help around the edges, but they aren't what turns a model into a playable game.
hints: Three jobs: make the art, run the game, write the code.
Map each tool to one of those three jobs — the extras don't fit any of them.
